items.followUp: State two examples of Newton’s third law of motion and identify the action and reaction in each.

rubric.why: One valid example of an action–reaction pair is given.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid third-law example.

rubric.why: A second valid example is given.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a different valid example.

modelAnswer: When we walk, our feet push the ground backward and the ground pushes us forward.
When a gun fires, the bullet moves forward and the gun recoils backward.

items.followUp: Define rotational motion and give one example.

rubric.why: The definition identifies the common motion of all parts of a translating body.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that all parts move the same distance in the same direction.

rubric.why: A suitable example demonstrates translatory motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid example, such as a car moving along a straight road.

modelAnswer: Translatory motion is the motion in which every part of a body moves the same distance in the same direction in the same time.
Example: A car moving along a straight road.

items.followUp: Draw a speed-time graph for a body moving with uniform deceleration.

rubric.why: The graph must identify time on the horizontal axis and speed on the vertical axis.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly labelled time and speed axes.

rubric.why: A straight line with positive slope represents uniform acceleration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a straight, upward-sloping line, with suitable points if a table is shown.

modelAnswer: Take time t (s) on the horizontal axis and speed v (m s⁻¹) on the vertical axis.
Use the representative values: t = 0, 1, 2, 3 s; v = 0, 2, 4, 6 m s⁻¹.
Plot (0, 0), (1, 2), (2, 4), and (3, 6), then join them with a straight line rising from the origin.

items.followUp: A bicycle speeds up from 2 m s⁻¹ to 14 m s⁻¹ in 6 s. Find its acceleration.

rubric.why: The initial velocity, final velocity and time interval are correctly identified.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the data and using a = (v − u)/t.

rubric.why: The correct acceleration is calculated with its unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for obtaining 5 m s⁻².

modelAnswer: Given: u = 0 m s⁻¹, v = 20 m s⁻¹, t = 4 s.
Substitution: a = (20 m s⁻¹ − 0 m s⁻¹)/4 s = 5 m s⁻².
Answer: The acceleration of the car is 5 m s⁻².

items.followUp: Write the formula for pressure at a depth in a liquid and name the quantities it depends on.

rubric.why: Pressure in a liquid increases with depth.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the depth of the liquid as a factor.

rubric.why: Pressure also depends on the density of the liquid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the liquid’s density as a factor.

modelAnswer: The pressure exerted by a liquid depends on the depth below its surface and the density of the liquid.
It also depends on gravitational acceleration: P = ρgh.

items.followUp: Define the moment of a force and distinguish clockwise and anticlockwise moments.

rubric.why: A moment describes the turning effect of a force.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining moment as the turning effect of a force.

rubric.why: The answer must distinguish the direction of the moment.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly defining clockwise and anticlockwise moments as turning effects in their respective directions.

modelAnswer: The turning effect of a force is called its moment.
A clockwise moment tends to turn a body clockwise about a pivot; an anticlockwise moment tends to turn it anticlockwise.

items.followUp: Define stable equilibrium and give one example.

rubric.why: In unstable equilibrium, a small displacement makes the body move farther from its original position.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for describing the body moving farther from its original position after a small displacement.

rubric.why: In neutral equilibrium, a small displacement leaves the body in its new position.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that after a small displacement the body remains in its new position.

modelAnswer: A body is in unstable equilibrium if a small displacement makes it move farther from its original position.
A body is in neutral equilibrium if, after a small displacement, it remains in its new position.

items.followUp: Resolve a force of 10 N acting at 30° to the horizontal into horizontal and vertical components.

rubric.why: The force is resolved into components at right angles to each other.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the force is split into two perpendicular components.

rubric.why: The components are related to the force and its angle by the appropriate trigonometric ratios.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining that the components are found using the force and the angle, with Fₓ = F cos θ and Fᵧ = F sin θ when θ is measured from the horizontal.

modelAnswer: Choose two perpendicular directions, usually horizontal and vertical, and resolve the force along these directions.
If the force F makes an angle θ with the horizontal, its horizontal component is Fₓ = F cos θ and its vertical component is Fᵧ = F sin θ.
